content.text: latest

is the tag Docker uses when you don't name one, not a promise about versions. It points wherever the last push of that name left it, and every machine resolves it at its own moment. A digest is the hash of the image's content and never moves, so deploy a version tag with its digest and every server runs the same image.
Version 1.4.0 ships on Monday. On Wednesday, a hotfix for a customer still on 1.3 goes out from the maintenance branch, and that pipeline, like every pipeline in the company, also pushes
latest
. On Thursday, the autoscaler adds two servers. They start 1.3.1, while the older servers keep running 1.4.0. Nobody deployed anything, and the dashboards show the same image name everywhere.
The common misconception
The belief:
latest
always points to the newest version of an image, so deploying
shop-api:latest
means deploying the current release, and it's safe.
It's a natural reading. The name promises it. Docker applies it for you: the
docker image tag
reference says "If no tag is provided, Docker defaults to
latest
." And in a team where one pipeline builds one branch, the last image pushed usually is the newest, so most days the belief holds.
The half-truth:
latest
is the most recently pushed image with that name, by whoever pushed it. Being the newest version is a habit of some pipelines, not a rule of Docker or the registry.
What actually happens
A tag is a name that can move
An
image tag
is a label on an image in a repository. Docker's best-practices guide is direct about it: "Image tags are mutable, meaning a publisher can update a tag to point to a new image." A push to
shop-api:latest
moves the name to the pushed image. Nothing compares version numbers or dates first. The same guide describes publishers moving tags like
to newer patch releases and adds that "most publishers use this tagging strategy, but it isn't enforced."
A digest is the image's fingerprint
An
image digest

identifies the content itself. The Kubernetes docs explain the difference in two sentences: "Digests are hashes of the image's content, and are immutable. Tags can be moved to point to different images, but digests are fixed." It's a SHA-256
hash
, so any change to the image gives a new digest. Docker shows it on every push and pull, and the
docker image pull
reference says that when pulling by digest, "you specify exactly which version of an image to pull."
Each machine resolves the tag when it pulls
A tag is turned into an image when a machine pulls it, not when you deploy. And
docker run
doesn't pull an image it already has: its default pull policy,
missing
, means "Pull the image if it was not found in the image cache, or use the cached image otherwise." A server that pulled
latest
last week keeps running last week's image. A new server pulls whatever
latest
is now. The Kubernetes docs warn about the result: "you might end up with a mix of Pods running the old and new code."
The fix: deploy the digest, not the name
We reproduced the hook with Docker 29.4.3 and a local
registry:3.1.2
on port 5055. Version 1.4.0 was pushed as
and
latest
; then the 1.3 hotfix was pushed as
and, like in the hook, as
latest
. To play a server that had pulled
latest
before the hotfix, we pointed its local
latest
tag back at 1.4.0:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# The 1.3 hotfix pipeline also moves latest
docker tag localhost:5055/shop-api:1.3.1 localhost:5055/shop-api:latest
docker push localhost:5055/shop-api:latest
# latest: digest: sha256:fdcd194b8298db4352335e4833b2febb6af2cff72f71341a0ff369b15897dc54 size: 668

# A server that pulled latest before that push
docker run --rm localhost:5055/shop-api:latest
# shop-api 1.4.0
# A server that pulls now
docker run --rm --pull=always localhost:5055/shop-api:latest
# shop-api 1.3.1

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# Keep the digest that the release push prints
docker push localhost:5055/shop-api:1.4.0
# 1.4.0: digest: sha256:f2437627542a2ecd3ea208d26ec8b508b7753ceb12ea39a2863f37c37a977c97 size: 668

# Deploy exactly that image on every server
DIGEST=sha256:f2437627542a2ecd3ea208d26ec8b508b7753ceb12ea39a2863f37c37a977c97
docker pull "localhost:5055/shop-api@$DIGEST"
# Digest: sha256:f2437627542a2ecd3ea208d26ec8b508b7753ceb12ea39a2863f37c37a977c97
docker run --rm "localhost:5055/shop-api@$DIGEST"
# shop-api 1.4.0

content.text: In the first tab, one name gave two answers. The hotfix moved
latest

from 1.4.0's digest to 1.3.1's: the newest push, not the newest version. The server with a cached copy ran 1.4.0 without asking the registry, and the server that pulled got 1.3.1. In the second tab, the pull ran on a machine with no copy of the image, after
latest
had already moved. It still got 1.4.0, because the digest names the content, and that content can't change.

By convention no, but the registry allows it

blocks.title: Keep the tag next to the digest

content.text: A digest alone tells a reader nothing. Write both:
shop-api:1.4.0@sha256:…
. The Kubernetes docs list this form and note that "Only the digest will be used for pulling", and Docker's best-practices guide pins
FROM
lines the same way. You keep a version people can read and a reference that can't move.

blocks.title: A pinned digest doesn't get security fixes

content.text: Pinning works both ways. The
docker image pull

reference notes that with a digest, "Docker does therefore not pull updated versions of an image, which may include security updates." Treat digest updates as changes: let a bot such as Dependabot propose new digests for your base images, as Docker's guide suggests, and ship them through your pipeline like any other change.
How to apply it in your project
Search your deploy scripts, Compose files and manifests for
:latest
and for images with no tag at all. The Kubernetes docs say to avoid it in production because "it is harder to track which version of the image is running and more difficult to roll back properly."

items.title: Tag every build with something unique

content.text: Use the release version or the commit SHA, and never push the same tag twice. Treat a reused tag as a bug in the pipeline.

items.title: Record the digest and deploy it

content.text: Save the digest that
docker push
prints with the build, and pass
image@digest
to the deploy step. A rollback then means deploying the previous digest, which still points at exactly what ran before.
Write
FROM
lines as
tag@digest
and let a bot open pull requests when the publisher moves the tag. Your builds stop changing under you, and the updates stay visible.
Key takeaways

items.text: is the default tag name, not a version: it points to whatever was last pushed with that name.
Tags are mutable; a digest is the hash of the image's content and can't move.
Each machine resolves a tag when it pulls, and
reuses a cached image by default, so one tag can mean different images on different servers.
Deploy by digest, ideally written as
, and roll back to the previous digest.
Pinned digests skip security updates, so update them on purpose through your pipeline.
